title: Italian Game
introduction: Take space in the centre, bring out a knight and bishop, then prepare your next central move. You will play one short, fixed line. The other side replies automatically.

lines.title: Prepare the centre
lines.description: Your first line: build towards a later d-pawn advance.

steps.hint: Move the pawn in front of your king from e2 to e4.
steps.explanation: The pawn takes space in the centre and opens a path for your bishop.

steps.hint: Move the pawn in front of your king from e7 to e5.
steps.explanation: Black also takes space in the centre.

steps.hint: Move your knight from g1 to f3.
steps.explanation: A knight comes towards the centre and attacks the pawn on e5.

steps.hint: Move your knight from b8 to c6.
steps.explanation: The knight develops and protects the pawn on e5.

steps.hint: Move your bishop from f1 to c4.
steps.explanation: The bishop develops to an active diagonal. This is the characteristic Italian setup.

steps.hint: Move your bishop from f8 to c5.
steps.explanation: Black develops a bishop too. Both sides are bringing pieces into play.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from c2 to c3.
steps.explanation: The pawn on c3 supports a later d2–d4 advance. You have reached the end of this short introduction.

steps.hint: Move your knight from g8 to f6.
steps.explanation: Black develops another knight and attacks the pawn on e4. This is the stopping point for this lesson.

lines.title: A quieter setup
lines.description: An alternative: support the centre with your d-pawn.

steps.hint: Move the pawn in front of your king from e2 to e4.
steps.explanation: The pawn takes space in the centre and opens a path for your bishop.

steps.hint: Move the pawn in front of your king from e7 to e5.
steps.explanation: Black also takes space in the centre.

steps.hint: Move your knight from g1 to f3.
steps.explanation: A knight comes towards the centre and attacks the pawn on e5.

steps.hint: Move your knight from b8 to c6.
steps.explanation: The knight develops and protects the pawn on e5.

steps.hint: Move your bishop from f1 to c4.
steps.explanation: The bishop develops to an active diagonal. This is the characteristic Italian setup.

steps.hint: Move your bishop from f8 to c5.
steps.explanation: Black develops a bishop too. Both sides are bringing pieces into play.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from d2 to d3.
steps.explanation: The d-pawn supports e4 and opens a path for the other bishop. This is a different taught line, not a chess mistake.

steps.hint: Move your knight from g8 to f6.
steps.explanation: Black develops another knight towards the centre. This is the stopping point for this lesson.

title: London System
introduction: Build a complete beginner London setup against a direct central response: develop both knights and bishops, support your centre with pawns, then castle. You play eight White moves; Black replies automatically along this one taught line. Other replies are possible in a real game.

lines.title: Build the London and castle
lines.description: Eight White moves: centre, development and king safety. One fixed teaching line against ...d5, ...Nf6 and ...e6.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from d2 to d4.
steps.explanation: Take space in the centre and open a path for the bishop on c1.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from d7 to d5.
steps.explanation: Black occupies the centre too. The d-pawns now face each other.

steps.hint: Move your knight from g1 to f3.
steps.explanation: Develop a knight towards the centre, where it helps control more squares.

steps.hint: Move your knight from g8 to f6.
steps.explanation: Black develops a knight and keeps an eye on the central squares.

steps.hint: Move your bishop from c1 to f4.
steps.explanation: Bring this bishop outside your pawn chain before playing e3, which would close its diagonal.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from e7 to e6.
steps.explanation: Black supports the pawn on d5 and opens a path for the bishop on f8.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from e2 to e3.
steps.explanation: Support your pawn on d4 and open a path for the bishop on f1.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from c7 to c5.
steps.explanation: Black challenges the pawn on d4. This is pressure on the centre, not a random pawn move.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from c2 to c3.
steps.explanation: Give the pawn on d4 another defender. Your c3, d4 and e3 pawns form a compact central structure.

steps.hint: Move your knight from b8 to c6.
steps.explanation: Black develops another piece and adds pressure to d4.

steps.hint: Move your knight from b1 to d2.
steps.explanation: Bring your remaining knight into play. It supports f3 and leaves c3 available for your pawn.

steps.hint: Move your bishop from f8 to e7.
steps.explanation: Black clears f8 so the king can castle, without immediately challenging your bishop on f4.

steps.hint: Move your bishop from f1 to d3.
steps.explanation: Develop your last bishop towards the centre. The squares between your king and rook are now clear for castling.

steps.hint: Castle: move your king from e8 to g8. The rook moves from h8 to f8 automatically.
steps.explanation: Black brings the king towards shelter and the rook towards the centre. Castling moves the king and rook together.

steps.hint: Castle: move your king from e1 to g1. The rook moves from h1 to f1 automatically.
steps.explanation: Your king moves towards shelter and your rook joins the game. You have built the London setup and castled. This is an opening foundation, not the end of the game.

title: Caro-Kann Defense
introduction: Play Black against 1. e4. Prepare ...d5 with ...c6, answer a central exchange, and bring your pieces into play. Start with a five-move Exchange setup, then try a longer Panov line ending in castling. White replies automatically along the selected line; real opponents can choose other continuations.

lines.title: First steps: the Exchange setup
lines.description: Five Black moves. Meet a central exchange, then develop both knights. This short foundation stops before castling.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from e2 to e4.
steps.explanation: White takes space in the centre and opens a path for the bishop on f1. The Caro-Kann is a reply to this first move.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from c7 to c6.
steps.explanation: Prepare to move your d-pawn to d5. From c6, this pawn will support that central advance.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from d2 to d4.
steps.explanation: White places a second pawn in the centre. Black will challenge that centre rather than leave it unopposed.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from d7 to d5.
steps.explanation: Challenge the white pawn on e4. Your pawn on c6 supports the pawn on d5: this is the central idea behind your first move.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from e4 to d5, capturing the black pawn.
steps.explanation: White exchanges the e-pawn for the black d-pawn. Pawns capture one square diagonally, rather than straight ahead.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from c6 to d5, capturing the white pawn.
steps.explanation: Recapture with the pawn you prepared on c6. The exchange is complete, and Black still has a pawn in the centre.

steps.hint: Move your bishop from f1 to d3.
steps.explanation: White develops a bishop towards the centre. Both sides now need to bring more pieces off their starting squares.

steps.hint: Move your knight from b8 to c6.
steps.explanation: Develop a knight towards the centre. It attacks the white pawn on d4 and controls the central square e5.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from c2 to c3.
steps.explanation: White gives the pawn on d4 another defender. This is a solid reply to the pressure from your knight.

steps.hint: Move your knight from g8 to f6.
steps.explanation: Develop your other knight towards the centre. You have learned the Caro-Kann pawn idea and brought both knights into play. This line ends here; your bishops and king still need attention in a real game.

lines.title: Next step: meet the Panov and castle
lines.description: Nine Black moves. White challenges d5 with the c-pawn; develop your pieces, recapture in the centre, then castle.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from e2 to e4.
steps.explanation: White takes space in the centre and opens a path for the bishop on f1. The Caro-Kann is a reply to this first move.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from c7 to c6.
steps.explanation: Prepare to move your d-pawn to d5. From c6, this pawn will support that central advance.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from d2 to d4.
steps.explanation: White places a second pawn in the centre. Black will challenge that centre rather than leave it unopposed.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from d7 to d5.
steps.explanation: Challenge the white pawn on e4. Your pawn on c6 supports the pawn on d5: this is the central idea behind your first move.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from e4 to d5, capturing the black pawn.
steps.explanation: White exchanges the e-pawn for the black d-pawn. Pawns capture one square diagonally, rather than straight ahead.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from c6 to d5, capturing the white pawn.
steps.explanation: Recapture with the pawn you prepared on c6. The exchange is complete, and Black still has a pawn in the centre.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from c2 to c4.
steps.explanation: White attacks the black pawn on d5 with another pawn. This central challenge is called the Panov Attack.

steps.hint: Move your knight from b8 to c6.
steps.explanation: Develop a knight and put pressure on the pawn on d4. You can bring pieces into play while White decides how to handle the central pawns.

steps.hint: Move your knight from b1 to c3.
steps.explanation: White develops a knight and adds another attack on the black pawn on d5.

steps.hint: Move your knight from g8 to f6.
steps.explanation: Bring your second knight towards the centre. Both black knights are now active instead of sitting on the back rank.

steps.hint: Move your knight from g1 to f3.
steps.explanation: White develops the other knight and adds another defender to d4. Moving it also clears g1 for later castling.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from e7 to e6.
steps.explanation: Support the pawn on d5 and open a diagonal for the bishop on f8. This prepares the next stage of your development.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from c4 to d5, capturing the black pawn.
steps.explanation: White exchanges the c-pawn for the black pawn on d5. Black now needs to recapture to restore the material balance.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from e6 to d5, capturing the white pawn.
steps.explanation: Recapture with your e-pawn and keep a pawn in the centre. Both sides now have a d-pawn without a friendly pawn on either neighbouring file, so pieces must help defend those pawns.

steps.hint: Move your bishop from f1 to b5.
steps.explanation: White develops a bishop and pins the knight on c6 to the king on e8: moving that knight would expose the king.

steps.hint: Move your bishop from f8 to d6.
steps.explanation: Develop your bishop on an open diagonal. With the bishop and knight out of the way, the squares between your king and h8 rook are clear for castling.

steps.hint: Move your bishop from c1 to g5.
steps.explanation: White develops another bishop and lines it up with the knight on f6 and queen on d8. This is pressure on a piece, rather than a check on the king.

steps.hint: Castle: move your king from e8 to g8. The rook moves from h8 to f8 automatically.
steps.explanation: Bring your king towards shelter and move a rook closer to the centre. Castling also takes your king away from the bishop pin on c6. This lesson ends with both knights and one bishop developed; the bishop on c8 still needs a plan.

title: French Defense
introduction: Learn one French plan against White's Advance Variation: support your centre, challenge d4 with your c-pawn, then develop pieces towards that target. You play seven Black moves; White replies automatically along this fixed line. Other White replies need different plans.

lines.title: Challenge the pawn centre
lines.description: Advance Variation: pressure on d4 with the c-pawn, knight and queen, followed by an exchange and bishop development.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from e2 to e4.
steps.explanation: White takes space in the centre and opens a diagonal for the bishop on f1.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from e7 to e6.
steps.explanation: Prepare to put the d-pawn on d5 with support from this pawn. This is the first move of the French Defense.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from d2 to d4.
steps.explanation: White builds a broad pawn centre. Black will challenge it rather than let both pawns advance freely.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from d7 to d5.
steps.explanation: Challenge the pawn on e4. Your pawn on e6 supports d5, so White cannot simply win that pawn by capturing it.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from e4 to e5.
steps.explanation: White advances instead of exchanging pawns. The central pawns now block each other; this is the Advance Variation.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from c7 to c5.
steps.explanation: Attack the pawn on d4, which supports White's advanced pawn on e5. Challenging the base of a pawn chain is a useful plan when the centre is blocked.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from c2 to c3.
steps.explanation: White adds another defender to d4. These connected pawns help hold the centre together.

steps.hint: Move your knight from b8 to c6.
steps.explanation: Develop a piece and add another attacker to d4. Your knight and c-pawn are working towards the same central target.

steps.hint: Move your knight from g1 to f3.
steps.explanation: White brings a knight into play and defends the advanced pawn on e5.

steps.hint: Move your queen from d8 to b6.
steps.explanation: The queen attacks b2 and lines up with d4. Your c5-pawn is still in the way; the queen will add pressure to d4 after that pawn is exchanged. This early queen move has a specific purpose.

steps.hint: Move your bishop from f1 to d3.
steps.explanation: White develops the bishop towards the kingside and clears f1 for possible castling.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from c5 to d4, capturing White's pawn.
steps.explanation: Exchange your c-pawn for White's central d-pawn. If White recaptures with the c3-pawn, your queen will have a clear diagonal from b6 to the new pawn on d4.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from c3 to d4, capturing Black's pawn.
steps.explanation: White recaptures and keeps a pawn on d4. Black still has a target for the knight on c6 and queen on b6.

steps.hint: Move your bishop from c8 to d7.
steps.explanation: Develop the bishop behind your central pawns and support your knight on c6. You have reached this lesson's stopping point: a French plan based on pressure against d4. Black still needs to develop the kingside and consider king safety as the game continues.

title: Queen's Gambit
introduction: Learn the Queen's Gambit as White against one declined response. Challenge the centre with c4, develop both knights and a bishop, then castle. You play seven White moves; Black replies automatically. The pawns keep their central tension in this line: capturing is a choice, not an obligation. This is one introductory line, not every possible Black response.

lines.title: Develop and castle
lines.description: Seven White moves against the Semi-Tarrasch symmetrical setup. Learn central pressure, development and castling without a forced pawn exchange.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from d2 to d4.
steps.explanation: Take space in the centre and open a path for the bishop on c1.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from d7 to d5.
steps.explanation: Black takes central space too and stops your d-pawn from moving straight ahead.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from c2 to c4.
steps.explanation: Challenge Black's central pawn from the side. This is the Queen's Gambit: Black could capture this pawn, but does not have to.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from e7 to e6.
steps.explanation: Black declines the offered pawn for now, supports d5 and opens a path for the bishop on f8.

steps.hint: Move your knight from b1 to c3.
steps.explanation: Develop a knight towards the centre and add pressure to Black's pawn on d5.

steps.hint: Move your knight from g8 to f6.
steps.explanation: Black develops a knight, supports the pawn on d5 and controls e4.

steps.hint: Move your knight from g1 to f3.
steps.explanation: Bring your other knight into play. It defends d4 and clears g1 for castling.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from c7 to c5.
steps.explanation: Black challenges your pawn on d4. Both sides now have pawns that could capture each other: this is central tension. Neither side must capture immediately.

steps.hint: Move your pawn from e2 to e3.
steps.explanation: Support d4 and open the diagonal for your bishop on f1. In this line you keep the central tension while developing.

steps.hint: Move your knight from b8 to c6.
steps.explanation: Black develops the second knight and adds another attacker to d4. The pawn on e3 and knight on f3 help you defend it.

steps.hint: Move your bishop from f1 to d3.
steps.explanation: Put the bishop on an open diagonal. With f1 and g1 clear, your king can prepare to castle.

steps.hint: Move your bishop from f8 to d6.
steps.explanation: Black develops the bishop towards the centre and clears f8 for castling.

steps.hint: Castle: move your king from e1 to g1. The rook moves from h1 to f1 automatically.
steps.explanation: Move your king towards the shelter of its pawns and bring the rook closer to the centre. Castling moves the king and rook together.

steps.hint: Castle: move your king from e8 to g8. The rook moves from h8 to f8 automatically.
steps.explanation: Black castles too. Both sides have developed knights and a bishop and sheltered their kings. This lesson ends here; the central pawn decisions and the rest of the game are still ahead.
